chunks: Eagle, Altium, KiCad, Allegro experience. The question: Do you have experience with Eagle/Altium/KiKad/Cadence Allegro?
The interviewer is asking which board-design programs you have really used, and whether you understand the steps every one of them shares.
Those steps are the same everywhere: draw the circuit, define the parts, lay out the board, check it, and send files to the factory.
A short, honest answer about one real board beats a long list of tool names.
It is like being asked which word processor you use. The real skill is writing; the programs differ mostly in menus and shortcuts.
A good answer names the program, says what you made with it, and admits which ones you have not touched. It also shows you could learn the team's program quickly.
The same loop exists in every tool.
The dashed arrow is the one that separates experienced designers: bring-up findings go back into the library and the checklists so the next board doesn't repeat the mistake.
ECAD: software for drawing circuits and designing circuit boards. Schematic: the circuit diagram, showing which parts connect to which.
Footprint: the pattern of copper pads on the board that a part is soldered onto. Layout: arranging the parts on the board and drawing the copper paths between them.
DRC (design rule check): an automatic check that the layout obeys the factory's limits, such as minimum spacing.
A similar check on the schematic is called ERC and catches things like unconnected pins. Gerber files: the standard files you send to the factory that makes the board.
Here is a skeleton to fill in with your own true details. "I used [tool] on [board] .
I made the footprints from the datasheets, drew the schematic and ran the checks, laid out the board with rules set to the factory's limits, and sent Gerber files.
When I first powered the board, I found [one mistake] , so I fixed [library or checklist] .
I have not used [other tools] , but the steps are the same, so I would learn the team's tool in a couple of weeks." Do not claim tools you have not used. That is the whole idea.
"I've used [tool] for [board] : library parts from datasheets, schematic with ERC, layout with design rules set to the fab's limits, DRC, then Gerbers, drill, BOM and pick-and-place.

I know the others conceptually: Eagle is simple and library-centric, Altium is integrated with strong rules and collaboration, KiCad is open source with Python scripting, and Allegro is the high-end constraint-driven tool.
The workflow is the same, so I'd ramp up on a new one in a couple of weeks."
